cloze.text: A white opacity shaped like an inverted "V" at the bottom of a panoramic image is called the {{c1::"shark fin"}} error; correct it by {{c2::lowering the lead apron}}.
A panoramic lead apron does {{c1::NOT}} have a thyroid collar.
cloze.extra: Book note under the shark-fin error. A collar would block the beam at the bottom of the image.

cloze.text: A ghost image is {{c1::magnified and blurry}} and appears on the {{c2::opposite}} side of the radiographic image from the real object.
cloze.extra: Correction: remove the object before exposure if possible.

cloze.text: A ghost image can also be produced by a body part, such as the {{c1::ramus}}.
For a metal foreign object (tongue ring, piercing, braces) on a panoramic image, the correction is to {{c1::remove the object prior to exposure}} if possible.

A white tapered opacity in the middle of a panoramic image is called the {{c1::Washington Monument}} error; correct it by having the patient {{c2::take a step forward, straighten the back/neck, and lean slightly back}}.
cloze.extra: Figure 2 in the book: straightened back position.

cloze.text: A large dark shadow over the maxillary teeth, between the palate and the dorsum of the tongue, is corrected by instructing the patient to {{c1::place the tongue on the roof of the mouth}} before exposure.

Thin, blurry anterior teeth with the spine visible on the sides of a panoramic image (biting too far forward) are corrected by making sure the anterior teeth are {{c1::in the grooves of the bite block}}.
cloze.extra: Same correction for biting too far back (fat, blurry anteriors).

cloze.text: When the patient's chin is tipped too far down or too far up, the correction is to position the {{c1::Frankfort}} plane {{c2::parallel to the floor}}.
cloze.extra: Book spells it 'Frankfurt'. The book's figure also shows the ala-tragus plane (blue) for comparison.

cloze.text: The Frankfort plane runs from the {{c1::bottom of the orbit}} to the {{c2::middle of the ear}} (book's definition).
Teeth and ramus wider on one side of a panoramic image (head twisted) are corrected by {{c1::centering the head's midline using the beam guides}}.
Condyles unequal in height (head tipped) are corrected by {{c1::repositioning the head using the machine's guidelines}} (midline beam guide).
Blurred portions and large defects on a panoramic image (patient movement) are prevented by instructing the patient to {{c1::hold still prior to and during exposure}}.

Radiographic prescribing guidelines are based on the patient's {{c1::dentition}}, {{c2::caries risk}}, and specific clinical needs, to optimize diagnostic information while {{c3::minimizing radiation exposure}}.
New patient, primary dentition: {{c1::selected periapical/occlusal views and/or posterior bitewings}}, recommended if proximal surfaces {{c2::cannot be visualized or probed}}.
A child new patient with no evidence of disease and {{c1::open proximal contacts}} may not require a radiographic exam, because child dentition is often spread out, allowing probe access.
New patient, mixed dentition, adolescent, or partially edentulous adult: {{c1::posterior bitewings with a panoramic exam}} OR {{c2::posterior bitewings and selected periapicals}}.
The mixed-dentition new-patient recommendation applies after the eruption of the {{c1::first permanent tooth}}.
New patient, edentulous adult: radiographic exams are based on {{c1::clinical signs and symptoms}}.
A new patient of any age with generalized dental disease or a history of extensive treatment: a {{c1::full-mouth intraoral radiographic exam}} is preferred.
cloze.extra: Extensive pathology or prior treatment means a greater need for diagnostic information.

cloze.text: For recall children/adolescents at increased caries risk, bitewings are indicated if proximal surfaces {{c1::cannot be examined visually or with a probe}}.
Radiographs should {{c1::not}} be taken every 6 months regardless of patient condition; determine the interval based on {{c2::caries risk}}.
For periodontal disease and for monitoring growth and development, {{c1::clinical judgment}} determines the need for and type of radiographic images.
cloze.extra: Perio: an individualized approach based on disease severity and progression.

cloze.text: Adolescents often require a {{c1::panoramic}} exam to monitor developing {{c2::third molars}}.
The incisive foramen is a small {{c1::radiolucent}} oval between the roots of the maxillary central incisors; it is the passageway for the {{c2::nasopalatine}} nerves.
cloze.extra: Should not be confused with periapical disease.

cloze.text: The median palatal suture is a vertical {{c1::radiolucent}} thin line in the middle of the palate.
cloze.extra: Should not be mistaken for a fracture.

cloze.text: On a periapical, the nasal septum appears as a {{c1::radiopaque}} vertical strip.
The {{c1::nasal spine}} is a {{c2::radiopaque}} triangular projection of bone anteriorly, at the median palatal suture where the nasal septum and fossae meet.
The nasal cavity (nasal fossae) appears as {{c1::radiolucent}} oval shapes superior to the {{c2::central incisors}}.
cloze.extra: Large air-filled space above and behind the nose in the middle of the face.

cloze.text: The maxillary sinuses are hollow spaces in bone superior to the maxillary {{c1::molars and premolars}}.
The {{c1::inverted Y}} is the junction where the {{c2::nasal fossa}} and the {{c2::maxillary sinus}} meet, most commonly superior to the maxillary {{c3::canine}} apex.
The maxillary tuberosity appears as a rounded {{c1::radiopaque}} elevation distal to the {{c2::third molar}} region.
The hamulus is an extension of the {{c1::medial pterygoid plate}} of the {{c2::sphenoid}} bone, seen as a radiopaque hook-like protrusion {{c3::posterior to the maxillary tuberosity}}.
The zygomatic process appears as a {{c1::U-shaped}} {{c2::radiopaque}} band superior to the maxillary {{c3::molar}} apices.
The {{c1::coronoid process}} (anterior portion of the ramus) is a radiopaque triangular projection usually superimposed over the {{c2::maxillary tuberosity}} on a maxillary molar periapical.
The genial tubercles appear as circular {{c1::radiopacities}} inferior to the mandibular {{c2::central incisor}} apices.
The lingual foramen is a {{c1::radiolucent}} circle inside the {{c2::genial tubercles}}; it is the exit for {{c3::incisive vessel}} branches.
The mental foramen is a round {{c1::radiolucent}} area inferior to the mandibular {{c2::premolar}} apices; it is the opening for the mental {{c3::nerve and vessels}}.
The mental ridge appears as bilateral {{c1::radiopaque}} lines that start inferior to the {{c2::premolar}} apices and extend anteriorly to the midline.
cloze.extra: Ridge of bone on the anterior surface of the mandible.

mcq.question: A panoramic image shows a white, inverted-V-shaped opacity obscuring the lower portion of the image. What is the most likely cause?
options: A. Patient's tongue was not on the palate
B. Lead apron was placed above the collar line
C. Patient's spine was slumped
D. Patient's chin was tipped down
mcq.answer: B. Lead apron was placed above the collar line
mcq.explanation: The 'shark fin' error is the lead apron blocking the beam; lower the apron (panoramic aprons have no thyroid collar). A slumped spine gives a white tapered opacity in the MIDDLE of the image (Washington Monument), not at the bottom.

mcq.question: A panoramic image shows a large dark (radiolucent) band over the apices of the maxillary teeth. Which instruction would have prevented this error?
options: A. Hold still during the exposure
B. Bite farther back on the bite block
C. Place your tongue against the roof of your mouth
D. Tip your chin down
mcq.answer: C. Place your tongue against the roof of your mouth
mcq.explanation: The air space between the dorsum of the tongue and the palate shows as a dark shadow over the maxillary teeth. Tipping the chin down would cause an exaggerated smile line instead.

mcq.question: On a panoramic image the teeth and ramus on the patient's right side appear much wider than on the left. Which statement is correct?
options: A. The patient's chin was tipped up
B. The head was twisted, and the right side was closer to the tubehead
C. The head was twisted, and the right side was closer to the receptor
D. The patient bit too far forward on the rod
mcq.answer: B. The head was twisted, and the right side was closer to the tubehead
mcq.explanation: A twisted head makes one side wider; the wider side is the side closer to the tubehead. Correct by centering the midline with the beam guides.

mcq.question: A 30-year-old recall patient with several teeth missing has had no clinical caries and is not at increased caries risk. When should posterior bitewings be taken?
options: A. Every 6 months
B. At 6–18-month intervals
C. At 12–24-month intervals
D. At 24–36-month intervals
mcq.explanation: Partially edentulous adult, no caries and no increased risk: 24–36 months. 6–18 months is for the same adult at increased caries risk; routine 6-month radiographs are never indicated.

mcq.question: A new adult patient presents with generalized dental disease and a history of extensive restorative treatment. Which radiographic exam is preferred?
options: A. Posterior bitewings only
B. Panoramic image only
C. Full-mouth intraoral radiographic exam
D. Exam based on clinical signs and symptoms only
mcq.explanation: Generalized disease or extensive treatment (any age) indicates a full-mouth intraoral exam. Posterior BWs + pano or BWs + selected PAs is the routine choice for adults without that history.

mcq.question: On a mandibular premolar periapical, a round radiolucency is seen below the premolar apices in an asymptomatic patient with vital teeth. This is most likely the:
options: A. Lingual foramen
B. Mental foramen
C. Incisive foramen
D. Genial tubercles
mcq.explanation: The mental foramen is a round radiolucency inferior to the mandibular premolar apices and is sometimes mistaken for periapical disease. The lingual foramen lies in the midline, inside the genial tubercles.

mcq.question: A radiopaque hook-like structure is seen posterior to the maxillary tuberosity on a molar periapical. It is an extension of which structure?
options: A. Zygomatic process of the maxilla
B. Coronoid process of the mandible
C. Medial pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone
D. Nasal spine
mcq.answer: C. Medial pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone
mcq.explanation: This is the hamulus, an extension of the medial pterygoid plate of the sphenoid. The coronoid process is a triangular opacity often superimposed OVER the tuberosity.
